text: You've drawn plenty of your own architecture diagrams by now. This lesson flips that around: given someone else's diagram, cold, in a design review, how do you read it the way a senior architect does — fast, skeptically, and in a way that produces real findings in the first few minutes? The habit to build is this: a diagram is a claim about how the system is supposed to behave, not proof that it actually behaves that way.

Don't start by reading every label. Pick one real request — a customer placing an order — and trace it arrow by arrow from entry point to data store and back. Watch for where one inbound arrow fans out to five services that can each independently fail the whole request. Watch for arrows that disappear into a box with no detail — is there pooling, caching, retry logic in there, or nothing? And watch for write paths with no visible return or retry route at all.

Second pass: find every trust boundary — any line where the level of trust changes, public internet into a private network, one account into another. Many real diagrams don't draw these explicitly, so part of the job is drawing them back in mentally. At every crossing, ask the same two questions: what actually enforces this boundary, and is that enforcement visible on the diagram, or just assumed?

Third pass: find the real failure domains. A box drawn around components doesn't prove they fail independently — what matters is the infrastructure underneath. Two services drawn as separate boxes that both depend on the same single-region database are in the same failure domain in practice, no matter how far apart the diagram draws them. That's the exact gap a diagram can hide visually while it's still true underneath.

Put all three passes together and you already have pillar findings without opening a single config file: a fan-out with no retry path is reliability; an unguarded boundary crossing is security; two boxes sharing one database is reliability again. That's the whole skill this chapter built toward — turning a picture into the same specific, pillar-anchored language you practiced across the last three lessons. From here, Chapter 2 puts this shared vocabulary to work on full capstone scenarios.
